scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Llamerada represents the historical journey of camelid herders and muleteers who traveled from the high Andean altiplano to lower valleys to trade products, utilizing the llama as their primary pack animal.

While certain researchers argue that the tradition holds ancient or Inca roots tied to pre-Hispanic Tahuantinsuyo and pastoral rituals, others locate its modern festive emergence in Bolivia's Oruro and Potosí regions.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Beyond its representation of herding and trade caravans, the Llamerada maintains historical ritual significance linked to Pachamama (Mother Earth) and livestock fertility.

It is performed in major religious and civic celebrations across the Andes, including the Carnaval de Oruro, the Fiesta del Gran Poder, the Festividad de Urkupiña, and the Festividad de la Virgen de la Candelaria in Puno.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The choreography of the Llamerada is executed by male and female dancers positioned in two separate, parallel columns.
Movements mimic the light, springy trotting motion of llamas traversing rugged mountain passes.

Dancers execute synchronized forward and backward steps, interweaving choreographic formations while twirling a khorawa (a traditional woven sling) in their right hand to rhythmically simulate herding signals.
Watch for Khorawa rotation.

Formation: Two long parallel lines (men and women separated) performing synchronized group turns and figures.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is set to a rhythmic, continuous meter designed to match a light trotting gait.
Traditional altiplano brass bands and native panpipe ensembles provide the melodic foundation, combining bright cadences with steady percussion beats.
Listen for the Brass band, Bombo, Zampoña.
The pulse is 2/4 at about 115 beats a minute.
Bright altiplano brass or panpipe melodies set against a firm, marching bass drum pulse supporting continuous light stepping.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear distinctive square cloth monteras (headdresses) trimmed with fringe, reminiscent of the traditional headwear of Aymara community leaders (Mama Talla).
Footwear consists of abarcas or ojotas.
Men wear wool or silk shirts, knee-length bayeta trousers, colorful woven sashes (chumpi), cayto socks, and a brightly pattern aguayo shawl wrapped across the chest paired with a coiled rope.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The 'Conjunto Tradicional Llamerada Zona Norte', founded in 1921 in Oruro, is documented as the oldest formal ensemble dedicated to this dance.
Lead figures within fraternities include the qañiachu, who guides the troupe's movements, and the tatalas, community figures of higher hierarchy traditionally wearing black attire.
The dance is actively performed across both Bolivia (notably in Oruro, La Paz, and Potosí) and Peru (specifically in the Puno region).

Rooted in pre-Hispanic Aymara and Quechua pastoral traditions, the Llamerada evolved from altiplano camelid herding routines into organized festival performance arts across southern Peru and western Bolivia.

wardrobe.from_sources: Dancers wear distinctive square cloth monteras (headdresses) trimmed with fringe, reminiscent of the traditional headwear of Aymara community leaders (Mama Talla). Footwear consists of abarcas or ojotas. Men wear wool or silk shirts, knee-length bayeta trousers, colorful woven sashes (chumpi), cayto socks, and a brightly pattern aguayo shawl wrapped across the chest paired with a coiled rope. Female dancers wear multiple layered polleras (petticoats), an aguayo draped across the torso, and a blouse. Some male performers carry plaster masks depicting puckered lips to symbolize whistling to the herd.
